utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Lisa Biersay on behalf of the Prosecution, and with me functioning as our Case Manager this morning is Ms. Indah Susanti, also with our intern who is Kay Hong Leung. And I apologise for this column, it's very difficult to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes. It comes at a price for having such a big courtroom. So good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell with Ms. Manal Tellawi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I was told there was an issue, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President. On Saturday, that is the day before yesterday, we received an e-mail with a proofing note which is customary. What is less customary is that attached to the proofing note was a rather lengthy series of corrections and additions to the witness's statement made apparently by the witness in an e-mail sent to the Prosecution on the 24th of January, 2013, so that was more than a month ago. In particular, there is a new meeting involving the witness and some members of the -- what he believes is the SBWS on around the 20th of April, 1992. This meeting is referenced in a document of which we do have disclosure and which was on the Prosecution list. That's certainly the case. But what we did not have prior to Saturday was any indication that this witness was going to talk about it, much less that he was going to add one particular rather negative observation about that meeting. So we say this is rather new. The e-mail was clearly disclosable to the Defence pursuant to Rule 66(A)(ii). We didn't get it. So I would suggest there's clearly been a violation of disclosure. Now, as to whether -- as to what kind of remedy there might be, it places us in a very difficult position. I'm not sure that this would be an appropriate situation to talk about removing or prevent -- not allowing the admission of this material, but I haven't had any opportunity to discuss it with my client. Now, he may not know anything about it, but I haven't had the opportunity to raise that. So I suppose the remedy that I would ask is that if I don't use the entirety of today for my cross-examination, although I do believe that's likely, that we hold the witness over until tomorrow morning, after I've had an opportunity to consult with Mr. Hadzic, and then I can ask any additional questions that may be necessary about this matter. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I agree with the summary given by Mr. Gosnell. What -- I would differ in the assessment of this meeting which is described in a admitted exhibit. The e-mail essentially -- we sent some materials to the witness beforehand because there were lots of potential exhibits for him, and after he looked at those exhibits he forwarded that e-mail as additions for discussion. And it should have been disclosed; I agree with that. So while I agree with that, the information in the e-mail is consistent with the previously disclosed document that identified the witness himself as being present for that meeting. So I have no objections to the witness being held over if Mr. Gosnell deems it appropriate in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. So be it. Anything else? Then we can bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, Mr. Hadzic is not here today. We will get --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he will be absent and we filed a motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It has been filed. Thank you very much. Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. Could you state your first and last name, your date of birth, and nationality, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my name is James Lubin, L-u-b-i-n. My date of birth is 26 March 1936. I am British by nationality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Lubin, you're about to make the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I must point out to you that you're exposing yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. May I ask you to give the solemn declaration now. The usher will hand you the text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Ms. Biersay, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lubin.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I take it from your response to me that you are able to hear me well?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you also hear me well from this microphone?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I can indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Are you comfortably seated?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Very comfortably. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lubin, could you describe for the Trial Chamber what position you held from approximately March to June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes. During that period I was assigned to the United Nations Protection Force in Yugoslavia with the acronym UNPROFOR. I was assigned to an area called Eastern Slavonia. It was one of four sectors of the United Nations protected areas in the former Yugoslavia -- actually, on Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In that regard, did you provide a written statement in July of 2012 regarding your tender as civilian affairs co-ordinator?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And before I address the statement specifically, could you describe to the members of the Trial Chamber what occupied most of your time in that position you describe.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes. What occupied me overwhelmingly were the forced population movements of local population. When I say "forced local population movements," I mean they were not planned by the population; they were made to move.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And those movements that occurred with -- from within your sector?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: From within the sector into Croatia proper.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention to the July 20, 2012, statement, did you sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I have a binder which I have shown Defence counsel and he has agreed that I can show it to the witness. So at this time if we could please give this binder that contains some of the documents that we will be using during the witness's examination. Thank you. And in order I will be discussing tab 1 then tab 4 for the Registrar's reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lubin, if you could -- now turning to tab 1 which is a statement that is before you, may I ask the Registrar to display on the screen for the assistance of the Chamber the English original of 65 ter number 5964.1. And you can either look at the hard copy of the document you have or on the screen, whichever's easier for you. Directing your attention to this first page, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, it's the witness information testimony I signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And do you recognise your signature on that page?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And turning to the next page, if we could, do you recognise any initials at the bottom of that page?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise my initials.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did you initial each of the pages of this statement at the time that you signed it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we could turn to the second-to-last page. After paragraph 91, do you recognise the initials on that page?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I do, they're mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you prepared and signed your statement in July of 2012, certain documents were attached to that statement at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You have been advised that only the first 19 pages of your statement, the ones that actually contain your words, that only that will be admitted and it will exclude the attachments. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I do understand that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Instead, you were asked to provide a supplement to your July 2012 statement which correlated the attachment numbers mentioned in your statement to the internal numbering system of the Prosecution. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, prepare and sign such a supplement?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when approximately did you sign that supplement, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I signed it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recall whether it was this year or last year?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: It was this year.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in preparation for your appearance today, have you had an opportunity to read and review both the 2012 statement and the 2013 supplement?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you reviewed your July 2012 statement, did you find anything that you thought was incorrect?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Apart from minor typographical errors, there was nothing substantive which would alter the statement in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, if I could direct your attention to page 6 which is paragraph 27.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, just one moment, please. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In the first line it says: "While in the Sector, I conducted and participated in regular meetings with the RSK and local Serb authorities ..." Directing your attention to the word "regular," do you have any modification to make to that word?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, I think it would be better if the word "regular" were deleted because "regular" gives the impression that they were held at certain times on certain days. They were sometimes called at a moment's notice when emergencies occurred. So it would be better to remove the word "regular."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now directing your attention to page 9, paragraph 43, right above that paragraph 43 there is a heading that's: "Witnessed expulsions from Dalj and Aljmas." Is there any modification that you would like to make to that heading?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, I think the word "witnessed" should be taken out and the village of Erdut also added.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now directing your attention to paragraph 70, which can be found on page 14, in that paragraph it details a letter you sent to the vice-president of the government of the Serbian region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, protecting the, one, changing of names of some villages in Sector East which contravened paragraph 17(b) of the UN plan for UNPROFOR's mission ..." Do you have any modification you'd like to make to paragraph -- to the words "paragraph 17(b)"?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, I think it would be better if it were just made "paragraph 17," that would clarify my point in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now turning to tab 4, may I please ask the Registry for 65 ter number 6390.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And this one will be on the screen, Mr. Lubin.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I recognise it to be an addendum to my original statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And do you recognise your signature on that page?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And on the next page do you recognise your signature on that page, if we could zoom out a bit?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And following -- underneath paragraph 2 is a table correlating the attachments in your statement to identification numbers on the document as well as identification numbers given to you by the Office of the Prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page, please. Do you also recognise any signatures on that page?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you previously said that you have been able to review the documents to satisfy yourself that the correlations are correct; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, they are correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, if you were asked questions about the material contained in your 2012 statement and your 2013 supplement, would you provide in substance the same information?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I would indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: With the previous corrections made, are these two statements truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter number 5964.1 under seal. There is a public redacted version that is listed as 5964.3. And we'd also tender the supplement which is 65 ter number 6390. So three exhibits, two are -- the first two are the same, one under seal version, one public redacted version, and the supplement to those two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Biersay, the public redacted version, is that .3?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: .2, forgive me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: .2. Okay. And why are they under seal?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: They're under -- there's some redactions that were required because of some Rule 70 conditions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- and these documents are referenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Admitted and marked, three documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 5964.1 shall be assigned Exhibit P1351 admitted under seal, and its public redacted version 65 ter document 5964.2 shall be assigned Exhibit P1351.1, while the 65 ter 6390 will be assigned Exhibit P1352, admitted under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That last one admitted under seal, Ms. Biersay?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No, it need not be admitted under seal because there's no reference to any specific Rule 70 issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So the last one not under seal. Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Turning now to tab 48, may I please ask the Registry for previously admitted Exhibit L2.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And that will appear in colour on your screen, Mr. Lubin.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Excuse me, before we go to that tab, could we go to what I believe is previously admitted Exhibit 233.140.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, could I have a tab number. I can't --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Tab 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And is it possible if we could zoom in on the right portion of the map a little bit for the witness. Okay. That should do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lubin, are you -- this is a map. Do -- are you familiar with the area depicted in this map?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what area is depicted in this map?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: This depicts part of the lower half of Sector East.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And in this portion of Sector East, are you familiar with the names of the villages depicted?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm very familiar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you describe what, if any, travels you did throughout the sector during your tenure?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe to the Trial Chamber whether or not you would travel throughout the sector?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, I would travel -- every day I would travel throughout the sector, various parts of the sector, depending what kind of emergency had emerged there overnight, and sometimes I would travel just to have a regular meeting with local officials in towns such as Ilok, for instance, and a couple of the other towns.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where were you --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Villages I should say, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where were you headquartered?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: We were headquartered in Erdut in -- towards the top of the map which is cut off.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we could ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Erdut is situated on the bulge there that goes out into the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Are you able to take that pen, electronic pen, and just put a spot next to the -- Erdut that you identified?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes. This is Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And make it bigger as well.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: We have two Erduts by [indiscernible] but --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: It was that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now in paragraph 8 of your statement you refer to the UNPROFOR's mission and now I'd like to turn to tab 48, which I hope will be previously admitted Exhibit L2.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The map that we previously saw is already admitted as P233.140 and there's no need to capture the markings by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lubin, this document - as you can see - is dated 11 December 1991, and you will note that it reads that it is the report of the Secretary-General pursuant to Security Council Resolution 721 (1991). Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could now go to page 10 of this -- e-court page of this document, please. And, Mr. Lubin, are you generally familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And now directing your attention to page 10.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: We appear to be on page 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The document itself is marked page 15 and in our electronic system it appears --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- as page 10.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No, it's very good to put that on the record. Now, what you're looking at is annex 3, and it is the concept for a United Nations peacekeeping operation in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to direct your attention specifically to page 11, which is the next page which on the document itself reads "page 16." Now, that is right above paragraph 8. It reads: "The United Nations Protected Areas." Directing your attention to paragraph 9, which I believe is the B/C/S 3 if that will assist.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And at paragraph 9 reads that: "There would be three UNPAs: Eastern Slavonia , Western Slavonia and Krajina ..." and that is written in November/December of 1991. Was that the reality that you had when you were deployed to Sector East?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, Eastern Slavonia was the area in which I performed my duties, but eventually one of the other protected areas, the Krajina, was subsequently divided into north and south, making a total of four UNPAs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The description given there for the borders of the Eastern Slavonia UNPA, could you read that and is that -- and let us know whether that's consistent with the area when you arrived or if -- tell us if it's different?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: That is consistent with the situation when I arrived, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So it included Beli Manastir; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And those parts of Osijek which lie east of Osijek city; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And villages in the eastern --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Part of --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- part of Vinkovci?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention to page 13, paragraph 15, and if you wanted to look at a hard copy you can go to -- in your binder it would be tab 48 that would help you to navigate a bit more.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So on the hard copy it will say page "18" on the top portion. Now, if we could focus on the bottom of that page to the heading "Demilitarisation of the UNPAs," it describes that there would be a timetable and the UNPAs would be demilitarised. Now, I'd like to point you to paragraph 15(a) which reads: "All units and personnel to the Yugoslav National Army (JNA) and the Croatian National Guard, as well as any Territorial Defence units or personnel not based in the UNPAs, would be withdrawn from them." My question to you: What was the status of withdrawal of the JNA and Territorial Defence units when you arrived in the sector in March of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: They were present. They had not withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Was there any withdrawal that happened while you were in the sector?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, towards the end of my tenure, I believe in late May, the units of the Yugoslav national army started to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you say "started" --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: And they did complete that withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Directing your attention to 15(b): "All Territorial Defence units and personnel based in the UNPAs would be disbanded and demobilised ..." Was that the case when you arrived to -- into the sector?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: No, it was very far from the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Because these so-called Territorial Defence unit and, indeed, paramilitaries seemed more armed day by day.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could direct your attention to page 19 of the document before you, and for us it will be page 14. And directing your attention to subsection (d). So on your page, Mr. Lubin, it says page 19 at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And can you see the subsection (d)?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And I'll read it. "All paramilitary, irregular or volunteer units or personnel would either be withdrawn from the UNPAs or, if resident in them, be disbanded and demobilised."

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: No, that's not true. They were never demobilised during my time and they were never withdrawn. Indeed, there was a large increase in the number of these irregular forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And right below that, if I could direct your attention to paragraph 16, that reads: "It would be the responsibility of each unit, before it withdrew or was disbanded, to remove any mines which it had laid while deployed in the UNPAs." Was that -- how does that compare to the reality you faced when you were in Sector East?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: We did begin to oversee the removal of mines, but I think it was a very slow process which certainly hadn't been completed before my tenure was up, which was the 1st of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: On the same page, directing you to paragraph 19, it's just under the heading that reads "local police forces." And the first sentence in paragraph 19 reads: "The maintenance of public order in the UNPAs would be the responsibility of local police forces who would only carry side-arms ..." Now directing my question to you: Does that accurately reflect the situation that you had in Sector East?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: No. My interpretation of "side-arms" would be something like a pistol or small weapon of that sort. It was quite common for all the so-called police - I wasn't sure that they were really policemen - to carry such weapons as Kalashnikovs, that type of heavy-duty weapon which would contravene this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, why do you say "I wasn't sure that they were really policemen"?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Through our civilian police, our United Nations civilian police, my contacts with them were full time, they would always comment to me that so and so was not a policeman because they knew nothing about basic police procedures. They gave me the impression that they'd either been former military men or some kind of guard who had been hurriedly converted into so-called policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were there any of these policemen whom you knew well on a professional basis whom you were able to confirm that they were police officers?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So some people you weren't quite sure whether or not they were police officers. Did you have contacts with people whom you knew were, in fact, police officers in their capacity in dealing with you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There were few. It became obvious to me certain police chiefs were very professional in their approach, but others weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, if we could please go into private session to address several Rule 70 documents that we have on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you describe events relating to the village of Miklusevci. The document that appears that you have in your binder is tab 100, 65 ter number 5945. Is that document familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I recognise it information I sent to my superior, Cedric Thornberry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And it reads: "Please be advised that the mayor of Vinkovci has telephoned to inform me that approximately 180 Rutheians from Miklusevci have been expelled." Now, is that word meant to be "Ruthenians"?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you explain to the Trial Chamber how frequent it was to receive such calls from the mayor of Vinkovci?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: It wasn't very frequent. This was a rare call. I was usually informed by -- let me retrace that. I would learn of an expulsion in a number of ways from our military observers, our police, and sometimes the local authority would arrive at my door-step and tell me that there was an evacuation or something like that going on in a certain area and I could witness it if I wished.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the last sentence: "Need guidance on how to handle return of expellees to homes already occupied." To what does that refer?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The very last sentence --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- "Need guidance on how to handle return of expellees to homes already occupied."

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, we simply didn't know how to handle that because in the rare, rare instances where a couple of people wished to stay, their houses were already occupied. So the normal result of this was that they too would be expelled because there was nowhere for them to live.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And these homes were occupied by whom, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: These were occupied by Serb refugees who had been driven out of Croatia, so we were told.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time we tender 65 ter number 5945.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P1355. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if we could now turn to tab 53 which is 65 ter number 5170.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you describe expulsions related to Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And I direct you to this document that reads: "Attempted Expulsion, Tovarnik." Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I recognise it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: This is a situation report. These reports would be sent at least once daily, maybe up to six times daily, depending on the number of incidents that occurred in the sector. Situation reports going to my supervisor Cedric Thornberry in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the second page of that exhibit it reads: "Please be advised that some 22 Croats travelling in a minibus from Tovarnik have been intercepted ..." Is that the expulsion that is referenced in paragraph 86 of your statement about Tovarnik?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time we'd move for the admission of 65 ter number 5170.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now turning --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P1356. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Sometimes I wait too long and sometimes not long enough. Forgive me. If we could turn to tab 101. Yes, tab 101 which is 65 ter number 5946.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lubin, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I recognise it to a short situation report from me again to my supervisor, Thornberry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, the subject is "Expulsion Tovarnik." And it reads: "We have now confirmed that some 40 persons were expelled from Tovarnik ... yesterday, 24 May, in the morning. "The expelled were driven out on tractors, 2 or 3 at a time through fields, this avoiding RussBat roadblocks." First of all, what is RussBat?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: RussBat is our Russian Battalion who were assigned to protect and patrol the southern half of the sector. BelBat was the Belgian battalion which was assigned to guard and patrol the northern part of our sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in your statement there is reference made to 22 expellees from Tovarnik being on bus -- being bussed out of the sector. This document describes 40 persons being expelled through tractors. Could you shed some light on whether we're talking about the same expulsion or two different expulsions?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: We're talking about the same village but with two different expulsions. And I draw your attention to the fact that these expellees were driven on tractors through the fields, actually, thereby avoiding any roadblocks that we'd set up to prevent that. The 22 expellees referenced in paragraph 87 were on a minibus when we intercepted them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time we'd move for the admission of 65 ter number 5946.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P1357. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, at this time if we could please return to private session to address some more Rule 70 documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lubin, directing your attention to page 8, paragraph 36 of your statement, you describe that the expulsion process was very well organised. What was the basis for that conclusion on your part?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yeah, they were very well organised because initially they used buses, local transport buses. Many people were present, some with clipboards with lists of people that were to be expelled. And it was obviously not a spontaneous event.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In that regard in describing these expulsions, are you able to describe for the Trial Chamber the atmosphere surrounding these expulsions in Sector East?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yeah, the -- the atmosphere was one of absolute terror on the part of those being expelled. On a couple of occasions I actually boarded vehicles and tried to speak with some of the expellees, asking them were they voluntarily leaving. They all said yes and they were all obviously not telling the truth. Most other women were old women, they were crying. There were a few children who were also distressed. There were signs of brutal treatment, bruises on people, bandages. We were always called to these meetings, if we were called at all or informed about them, when it was too late for us to do anything about it. We would ask the people did they want to return to their homes. We would try to protect them. I can't recall one person who wished to return to their home. They were in absolute terror. It was extremely frustrating for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lubin.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am looking at the clock and it appears that it may be time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Biersay. Thank you. Mr. Lubin, we'll take our first break. We'll come back at 11.00. You will be escorted out of the courtroom by the court usher. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Biersay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I rise to inform the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution has no further questions for this witness and at this time we would tender his associated exhibits that are attached to the motion for his -- the admission of his statements pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: A memo will be circulated by the Registrar. Yes, they're admitted of course. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lubin.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My name is Christopher Gosnell, I represent Mr. Hadzic here, and I first off want to thank you for your long and distinguished service to the United Nations, obviously in some very difficult places. Now, I want to return to something you said this morning and that was in referring to policemen that: "I wasn't sure that they really were policemen." Did you find in your time in Sector East that there were individuals who were appropriating for themselves certain positions or titles when, in fact, they had no such authority? They had no authority to do so?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, this was not only my opinion but it was the opinion of professional police officers assigned to UNPROFOR, namely, our Swedish Battalion of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you find in particular that there were individuals who may previously have been involved in combat either as what would be described as volunteers or paramilitaries who then sought to describe themselves as police?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I personally was not aware of that, but -- could you rephrase the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I could put it shortly like this: As you travelled to some of the municipalities away from Erdut, for example, did you find that people were acting like police even though no one had appointed them to that position?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Well, there were active police. I really can't say whether anyone had appointed them or not, no, I couldn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look at a document and contextualise this.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we could have Prosecution tab 67 which is P1353 which should not be broadcast but perhaps we don't need to go into private session. We'll just look at the substance of this document and this particular portion of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I normally would agree to that, but the provision is that the document be discussed in closed session, that's the Rule 70 condition that we've been given.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, if that's the condition, that's what we'll have to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And this is Prosecution tab 21 if I can get to it in my own binder.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be 65 ter 5163. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Could we have page 7, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, this appears to be a document from Mr. Johansen to Mr. Thornberry dated the 22nd of February, 1992, and I believe this is in relation to the same incident we're discussing now, the Tovarnik alleged expulsion. And the paragraph I am interested in is the third or fourth paragraph from the bottom: "Regarding the expulsion on 18th May, 1992 - when the bus reached the check-point - the situation had reached what I would call the point of no return."

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, that is not the same expulsion. This is on the 18th of May. The Tovarnik expulsion you referred to before was on the 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Apologies, that's correct. In any event, this is another event --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- and do you see that characterisation, the point has -- "the situation has reached what I would call the point of no return"?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is that a fair characterisation of the state of affairs at the time?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I think that's a very fair characterisation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the next paragraph says: "To at least try to prevent further expulsion of people, it is necessary to show a massive presence based on information by CIVPOL in the area - the resources in Sector East - RussBat area are now released for this purpose." Do you recall that, in fact, really a -- notwithstanding what you said earlier about the UN relying on moral suasion and moral motivations that nonetheless really a major armed presence would be required in order to suppress the kind of violence that was encouraging people to leave?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, that would be my personal opinion, but referring to this paragraph the massive presence he refers to is just massive visibility. Unfortunately, we have -- we did have a problem with patrols in the southern part of the sector. To my mind, the Russian Battalion were not patrolling the area properly. Referring to this document that you've put on the screen, this is a visit the United Nations chief of police and myself made to the Russian Battalion to urge them to ensure that there were more patrols. We were not satisfied that they were doing enough or their presence certainly wasn't visible enough to prevent these kinds of incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And isn't that because the people who were creating the conditions of instability were well armed?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I don't follow your question, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, isn't it because the individuals who were threatening these civilians, inducing them to leave, the reason a very significant presence would be required is not because these were individuals throwing rocks or pebbles or hitting people with sticks and stones; we're talking about people with armed -- people with rifles. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that kind of opposition isn't going to be lightly overcome, is it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, but our job is always negotiation not confrontation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May I tender this document, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I add something to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Lubin. The Registrar tells me that this document is already admitted under 92 ter list, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you kindly. I had not realised that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lubin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I want to clarify that this was a United Nations peacekeeping mission. It was not a United Nations peacemaking mission. During the -- my some 25 years of service with the United Nations, there was rarely a peacemaking mission. I can only recall one and that was in Somalia. Normally the conditions have to exist in an area where there is peace to keep. Unfortunately, events showed that in this area there was no peace to keep.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have Prosecution tab 27 , please, which is 05924.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And coming up on screen in front of you, sir, is a sitrep from you to Mr. Thornberry and this concerns an event in Beli Manastir on 17 April, which you do describe in your statement. I won't ask you to go through all the details of that. In this statement at point 3 you say: "Two Hungarian families who had complained to CIVPOL - Beli Manastir of threats and violent acts against them from local were escorted and assisted in crossing the Batina bridge since they had declared their desire to return to Hungary. ICRC also assisted in this process." Would this again be one of those circumstances where you would say you'd made the determination that these individuals genuinely needed or wanted to leave?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, the determination was actually made by another civil affairs officer, Adnan Abd-Elrazek, who had arrived in the area and became responsible for the northern part of our sector. He relayed information to me about this family and I accompanied him together with the ICRC in this process. We were very moved by this family. They had young children. It was a typical expulsion. The car was heavily laden with personally belongings and I didn't actually go to the border of Hungary. I just escorted them out of the sector across the Batina bridge where the ICRC took over, and the children in the car before they left gave us a bunch of daffodils picked from their garden. I remember it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And these families were forced to leave without the vast majority of their belongings; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, in fact, weren't they leaving with the clothes on their backs and small bundles or parcels of belongings?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: That's correct. In a car, actually, in a car, their own car.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The fact that they didn't have all of their belongings didn't mean that you shouldn't assist them. In fact, the fact that they had fled just with the clothes on their backs was an indication that the situation was urgent; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes. This was not a rapid departure. They had told Mr. Abd-Elrazek a couple of days before that they wanted to leave. So they had a few more belongings than would normally take place when the expellees had not been given any notice that they were going to have to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It says here in this report that their departure was not without incident but the two families and three heavily laden small cars were then assisted to the Hungarian border by ICRC. Did someone attempt to block them from leaving?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Paramilitaries. And even the Yugoslav army. I think there were two instances, separate instances, where I had to talk them a way through barriers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were they blocking the departure of these individuals because they were afraid of being accused of engaging in expulsion of civilians?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: You'd have to ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I didn't discuss it with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did Mr. Abd-Elrazek discuss it with them and tell you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: We didn't discuss it with them. We just told them what we wanted to do and asked for free passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And no indication as to why they would try and stop you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you ever hear from any of the individuals that you assisted that they were waiting precisely for UNPROFOR's arrival so that they could leave the area because they previously had been prevented from leaving, whether by the JNA or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was a list made of the individuals in these three cars, either by you or by Mr. Abd-Elrazek?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: That would have been -- civilian police would do that. There was co-ordination always with civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember whether anyone as part of this convoy to Batina bridge was armed or was it just unarmed UNCIVPOL individuals as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: In this particular instance it was Mr. Abd-Elrazek and myself and that was all. No other -- I beg your pardon. I think we had a civilian police officer with us. I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm done with that document. I'm not sure whether this is an associated exhibit or not, if not I would tender it. It is an associated exhibit. Thank you. I'm done with the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Just, excuse me, if I can be of assistance, all the tabs essentially from 1 through 39 are part of the associated exhibits, if that assists.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Tremendously. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You say in your statement that there were 33.000 Serb refugees in Sector East who had themselves been expelled or at the very least fled from other parts of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes. I can't be absolutely sure about the number, but there is certainly an approximation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And based on your observation, were these individuals angry about what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: It was very, very difficult for me to know who was Serb refugee and who was a local Serb. During several public briefings, Serbs would tell me their side of the story. They would relate their situation where they true had been expelled from Croatia. In fact, some of the stories were quite moving. So I was aware that there was anger in some cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would you say that the presence of what I would characterise as such a large number of refugees or internally displaced persons, to be technically correct, created a situation of volatility in the area?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, I would say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, earlier today you said "certain police chiefs were very professional in their approach but others weren't." Can you recall which police chiefs would you recall were very professional in their behaviour?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, it was a small minority. I can recall one in particular. He was the chief police of Ilok. He was very open, and in my opinion he was honest. But he was unique. I believe he was a Croat married to a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let's go to Prosecution tab 82, which is 05903. I suggest to you, sir, that perhaps there were some other police chiefs who certainly at the time you thought were making their best efforts to tamp down a difficult situation. And if we go to page 3 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This should be in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we can go to page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is your report to Mr. Thornberry regarding your trip to Beli Manastir on the 22nd of April, and here you also confirm, as you've just said: "Beli Manastir officials made it clear they want a permanent civilian presence in Baranja and hope to hold similar meetings to discuss civil affairs issues. Local police admitted that extremists were responsible in civilian affairs working group meeting." Do you recall that working group meeting specifically?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yeah, I recall the meeting, but I can't say accurately what was discussed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "Civilian authorities said expulsion order was a forgery, co-operation again promised, usual problem: Orders not followed at lower level ..."

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, where is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Down at the very bottom of page 3, if we could just scroll down.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes. "Local police admitted that extremists were responsible in civilian affairs working group meeting. Civilian authorities said expulsion order was a forgery ..." Perhaps I should just stop here and situate this. You say in your statement that there was an alleged expulsion order for individuals and the -- the civilian authority here, am I correct, is denying that that was issued by them; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Okay. And then they say: "Co-operation again promised. Usual problem: Orders not followed at lower level." What are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Again, I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, it's the very last line of the page --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Ah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- which I think is now there.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yeah, I think I'm referring to the police giving orders and they weren't followed at the lower level.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what do you mean by in the first instance the police and in the second instance the lower level?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: The police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, who are you referring to precisely in this context, which police?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I think I'm referring to the local police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And who are you saying here is not following those orders?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: The local police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So to summarise, does that mean you're saying the local police chief is trying to give orders and that individual policemen are not following them; is that the gist of this or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: That appears to be the gist of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, given that you have here a police chief who wants to have a civilian UN presence in his jurisdiction, he's admitting frankly that there is this violence occurring, he's admitting that extremists are committing it, and he does - according to you - in the last line he does appear to be giving orders to -- at least to the best of his ability to tamp down these problems?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Why do you say he's being duplicitous?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: At what date was this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, you've written this report on the 22nd of April and --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: This report -- the sitrep?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And it may be the same day. In any event, sometime around the 22nd of April because I know how prompt you are about reporting events in your documents?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Yeah, I probably say that he's being duplicitous now because these are things that I learned as the mission went on, that whatever police officials told me I had to take with a grain of salt.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Doesn't it occur to you that in this context - and you surely were aware that there was instability in this region - and why do you discount the possibility that he was not being honest in asking for CIVPOL to be there, in asking for assistance, and in telling you quite frankly that this violence was going on and he wasn't able to stop it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: In this area nothing was ever what it seemed. There were always lies and counter lies. He may well have been telling the truth, but by this stage in the mission I was very skeptical about everyone. Frankly, I can't recall this conversation accurately or the meeting accurately. This is 21 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'd like now to turn to the Vance Plan and that's L2, Prosecution tab 48. Because I'd like, if possible, to try and look at who is responsible for what in Sector East during these important -- this important time-period. And if we could go to paragraph 7 of the annex which is -- it says page 16 on the page. I believe this is page 11 in e-court. And here we have the basic concept set out. And it says: "United Nations troops and police monitors would be deployed in certain areas in Croatia, designated as 'United Nations Protected Areas.' These areas would be demilitarised; all armed forces in them would be either withdrawn or disbanded. The role of the United Nations troops would be to ensure that the areas remained demilitarised and that all persons residing in them were protected from fear of armed attack ..." Now, let's just stop there. I think you'd agree with me that what we have is a clear obligation on the part of UNPROFOR to prevent remilitarisation of the area once it has been demobilised; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: It doesn't say that, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "The role of the United Nations troops would be to ensure that the areas remained demilitarised ..."

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So that's correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, you'd agree that this paragraph doesn't say who is responsible for actually compelling demilitarisation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: There again, this is a peacekeeping operation, not a peacemaking operation, so there was no compelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Except UNPROFOR is responsible here to ensure "that the areas remained demilitarised."

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, but UNPROFOR was not authorised to use force in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So they have an obligation that you're saying they may not be able to fulfil? I withdraw that question. If we could go down to page 15 in e-court and it's paragraph 15 of the annex. Now, down at the bottom we have the section starting "demilitarisation of the UNPAs." And here's what that says: "On the basis of the agreed timetables, demilitarisation of the UNPAs would be implemented as rapidly as possible, in the following way ..." In the first instance it says: "All units and personnel of the Yugoslav National Army ... the Croatian National Guard, as well as Territorial Defence units or personnel not based in the UNPAs, would be withdrawn from them. "All Territorial Defence units and personnel based in the UNPAs would be disbanded and demobilised. Disbandment would involve the temporary dissolution of the unit's command structures." (C), and this is, I would suggest, a crucial one: "The weapons of the Territorial Defence units and personnel based in the UNPAs would be handed over to units of JNA or the Croatian National Guard, as the case may be, before those units withdrew from the UNPAs ..." Does it appear to you looking at that that implies an obligation on the part of the JNA to enforce, if necessary, demobilisation of, and it's described I think very clearly here, Territorial Defence units and personnel?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes. I would just add a rider to this that most of the military matters were dealt with by my United Nations military colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Except that you met with General Biorcevic, the commander of the 12th Corps quite frequently; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Why did you meet with him so frequently?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Because he wanted me to meet with him in the first instance and he was the only legal authority as far as I knew. The so-called local administration was not recognised as official by the United Nations, but of course we had to deal with them because they were de facto.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: De facto what? I'm sorry, I thought you were going to say something else?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: They were de facto authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When you say "de facto authorities," are you saying that the JNA were the ones with the practical capacity and the only ones with practical capacity to enforce security in this area, in Sector East? And I'm talking about before the arrival of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And during the transition time while RussBat was coming up to strength, really it was still also only the JNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In fact, you refer in your statement to unoccupied Croatia, and I believe you may use the term "occupied Croatia," but you certainly do use the term unoccupied Croatia. Was it your view that Sector East, at least the areas in which the JNA was present, was occupied by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we go to Prosecution tab 29 which is 05929.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, can you give a general -- before looking at this document, can you give me a general idea of how frequently you did meet either with General Biorcevic or with any JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: A general idea. Certainly on arrival I met with him quite frequently because I was shuttling backwards and forwards from the sector to the Croatian side, and whatever comments the Croatian side made to me I would relate to General Biorcevic and vice versa. I was communicating their different opinions on various matters. So I met with him frequently earlier in the mission. As the mission went on, I met less and less frequently with him. I met after that mainly with the Krajina representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, at -- by the way, did you ever meet the head of the military police of the 12th Corps?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the rank but it was a Kosutic?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: He's -- probably attended by initial reconnaissance meetings. I had two initial reconnaissance missions at the beginning of March, early in March, when there were a large number of military men present on General Biorcevic's vessel which was tethered in the Danube. He may well have been amongst those officers, but I don't recall meeting with him certainly on -- not on a regular basis after those initial meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we could look at page 3 of the document there on the screen in front of you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It says - and this is the 19th of April - and this is in reference to as you say here in paragraph 1 "last night's expulsions from Dalj." Then you go down to paragraph 3 and that's what I'm --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I'm on page 2 here so could you go back.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There are only two pages of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry page 1, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, it's paragraph 3 that I'm interested in. It says: "As we were unable to meet with top JNA officials, JNA liaison officers were informed. They were also informed of the looting of 20 Croat houses in," it could be Torjanci, I'm not sure, "by JNA soldiers (see CIVPOL report). UNPROFOR's position on lack of JNA control over above was made clear." Now then if we can go over to page 2, paragraph 6. "From the above you will again see that JNA is losing control both of its own soldiers and other paramilitary units. Evidence given in the Dalj incident shows that such paramilitary were involved." Now, I'm interested in that formulation in paragraph 6 that you used: "From the above you will again see that JNA is losing control both of its own soldiers and other paramilitary units ..." Now, was it your view that the paramilitary units at this time, as of the date of that report, 19th of April, were under the de facto control of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I wouldn't characterise it as that, but they certainly had influence over them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was it your view that they should have control over those paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: No, I don't think I should have an opinion on that. I can tell you that people I believe were part of the paramilitary operation were present at some of those earlier meetings that I mentioned to you before, early in March. There were vast numbers of soldiers in irregular uniforms there. Some of them even had hand-grenades hanging from their shoulder straps, which I don't think is a regular military uniform procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was that at the meeting on the ship in the Danube?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Those paramilitaries were present there?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. I believe so because their uniforms were not regular.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, the reason I'm asking you these questions, you say it's not for you to say, we're discussing the Vance Plan --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- and I'm trying to get an understanding of who was responsible for what as envisaged by the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what we have in 16 -- excuse me, in paragraph 15(c) is a statement that "weapons of the Territorial Defence units and personnel based in the UNPAs," and I suggest to you that the reference to personnel based in the UNPAs is a bit of euphemism in diplo-speak for paramilitaries --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That -- that interpretation may be unique to Mr. Gosnell, but the witness is not required to adopt it. So if Mr. Gosnell would like to ask the witness if he agrees with that, that would be another thing. But I object to him incorporating it in his question in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to L2. Keeping in mind, sir, what you've just seen in paragraph 6 of your report, let's go back to L2 and have a look at the Vance Plan. And that's page 19 of the annex.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'll read it but it's coming up in front of you. "The weapons of the Territorial Defence units and personnel based in the UNPAs would be handed over to units of JNA ..." What do you understand the reference to "personnel based in the UNPAs" to be?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sure. It says there at the beginning of the sentence, this is about who -- to whom may weapons be given that are demobilised. And at the beginning of 15(c) it clearly says that the weapons of the Territorial Defence can be given to the JNA, and then there's a second group identified. And it says: " ... and personnel based in the UNPAs ..."

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Well, I'd think that was -- be paramilitaries. I would -- I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you. And -- and you say in paragraph 6, if we can now go back to 05929, please, page 2. And I apologise for flipping back and forth between these documents, sir. "From the above you will again see that the JNA is losing control both of its own soldiers and other paramilitary units ..." So here we have an apparent role for the JNA in demobilising these paramilitary units. We have the paramilitary units, according to you, being present on the JNA ship in the Danube. Are you saying in this paragraph that at this time you viewed the JNA either as de facto in control or that if they weren't in control they must be in control? Is that the view of the -- of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Let me read that question again. Officially the JNA were in control.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Officially and in substance true?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And as far as the Vance Plan is concerned, that's who has to be in control of demobilising these groups; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, but you know there was a -- further memorandums, additions to the Vance Plan, spelling out in more detail the demilitarisation of these units. And I believe in that further document it doesn't say anything about weapons being handed over to the JNA. I think you'll find that those weapons were supposed to be put under the control of both our military and local authorities with a lock -- with keys belonging to ourselves, when I say ourselves, I mean our military and the local authorities. So this previous document was superseded.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We're going to come to that change.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But before we -- I'm not planning on coming to this other document right now --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- but as we -- but while we're on the subject, when you say that there was a double-lock system and that one of the keys was to be held by the local authorities --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- do you recall that, in fact, it wasn't the RSK or the SBWS that was supposed to control one of those keys, it was, in fact, the local opstina. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: You may well be right, but these -- this is a military aspect of the mission. I did not deal with any of the military aspects of the mission. I relied purely on the military commanders we had there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's go back to L2, please. And let's move away a little bit from the military, but, sir --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: May I just add --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, if I can just situate the reason why I'm asking these questions. I want to situate the police questions within the broader context of the military questions, and I think you'd agree that it's not possible to discuss one without the other; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have page 12 of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But may I make a further explanation on this Security Council document that you've referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I did not operate under the instructions in that document because it was amended by further documents which clarified the duties of both civilian personnel, military personnel, and our civilian police. There spelled out in much more exact terms in that further document which we do have because I've seen it. I don't know the number, but I'm sure you can find out which one it was. So really, this document that you've been pointing me to is a bit of a red herring.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, with respect, I don't think it's a red herring, but in any event we will discuss the subsequent amendments to the plan. If we could look at paragraph 10 and now we're going to move over to the police, it says: "The function of protecting the inhabitants of the UNPAs would be shared between the United Nations Forces infantry units and its civilian police monitors. The infantry would ensure that the UNPAs remained demilitarised ..." We were discussing that earlier. And then it says: "The police monitors would ensure that the local police carried out their duties without discrimination against any nationality and with full respect for the human rights of all residents ..." And then at paragraph 12 it says the civilian police monitors would be unarmed. And then if we go to page 14, paragraph 19: "The maintenance," and this is the critical portion: "The maintenance of public order in the UNPAs would be the responsibility of local police forces who would carry only side-arms ..." Is that correct that they were legally not permitted to carry more than side-arms?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that wouldn't be enough, would it, to keep control of paramilitaries who were intent on destabilising the situation, would it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I don't think I'm qualified to comment on that.
