utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, you were there?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You saw the types of people who were committing these acts, groups of paramilitaries with rifles. Would you say that police carrying side-arms would have been in a position to stop them?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Well, some of their own policemen were involved in these expulsions, so they would be their own men.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Some people who you said earlier were claiming to be police but who may not have been; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lubin, we'll take a second break. We come back at 12.45. You will be escorted out of the courtroom by the court usher. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, at page 66 of the transcript it is about the demobilisation the weapons of the Territorial Defence units and personnel based in the UNPAs would be handed over to the units of the JNA. And you asked the witness what do you understand the reference to personnel based in the UNPA to be. And then you say -- it says that -- it says there at the beginning of the sentence: "This is about to whom weapons may be given that are demobilised and at the beginning of 15(c) it clearly says that the weapons of the Territorial Defence can be given to the JNA and then there is a second group identified." And it says, "and personnel." And then you get the answer I suppose you wanted to get, but could we go to L2, the document, and this was on page -- let's see -- where is it. You could perhaps help me where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, it's -- on the page it says page 19 of the annex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: On the page it says 19. Yes, there it is. Now could we go to page 18 where under (a) and (b) it is said all units and personnel of the Yugoslav National Army and in (b) all Territorial Defence units and personnel based in the UNPA; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Would you -- is it your understanding that each time where it is said "personnel" here it is referred to paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I believe so, but I do think it's a matter of evidence. My reading is that that is, indeed, the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: My problem is, Mr. Gosnell, that you suggest to the witness that it is a separate category. Shouldn't you first have asked him whether he considers it a separate category and eventually allowed him to read the rest of the text, because I think a plain reading means that it is the TO, all units and its personnel?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I now understand where you're -- that reading, Mr. President. I had not read it that when I put it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But I'm more than happy to be fair to the witness to then go back and let him say otherwise, because I did not intend to force him into that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm very happy to hear that, Mr. Gosnell, because I was under the impression that this could be something that could be considered as cross-examination skill in common law but would be much less be appreciated by a civil law judge. So I'm happy with your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I had no intention to do that. I genuinely had read it as two different categories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But I entirely see what you're reading too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be possible to save time to bring L2 -- oh, it's already on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Lubin, if I may, I'd like to go back to a subject that we have already discussed and I want to give you an opportunity, a full opportunity, to think about whether or not there's an answer that I may have pushed upon you a bit too strongly, and it concerns -- if we go over to the next page on this document in front of you, again coming back to this formulation "the weapons of the Territorial Defence units and personnel based in the UNPAs ..." I hate to belabour this but I do want to be fair to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It is possible that what is being said here is it's the units and personnel of the TO who -- whose weapons are being handed over to the JNA. That's a fair and possible reading, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: You're asking me that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry to have to ask it, but I made a mistake in pushing it on you too strongly, so now I'm giving you the opportunity to say otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: The wording in this document was superseded by a further document clarifying the role of everyone in the mission. It was much simplified, so that paragraph is irrelevant. I'll be pleased to answer questions on the updated version of the plan, the one that we used as our Bible in the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let me just ask you to -- for your patience for one additional question on this document before we move on, because after all this is the precursor at the very least to the document that you're referring to. And down at (d) it does say "all paramilitary, irregular, or volunteer units or personnel would either be withdrawn from the UNPAs or if resident in them be disbanded and demobilised."

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, again, I don't know what the version is in the other document because I don't have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's move now to Prosecution tab 26, please. This is 05919. If we could look at subparagraph (b), page 5. Now, this appears to be the press briefing that was given by Mr. Eckard around the 14th of April. Would you say that this accurately reflects what -- the Vance Plan as it was implemented? And, sir, I'm not asking you for a provision-by-provision analysis; that's a general question.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So it does reflect the Vance Plan as --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, if we just look at paragraphs (a) and (b), it again refers to the withdrawal of JNA and Territorial Defence units or personnel.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Then it says: "All Territorial Defence units and personnel based in the UNPAs are to be disbanded and demobilised ... demobilisation means that the personnel involved would cease to wear any uniform or carry any weapons, though they could continue to be paid by the local authorities." I assume you wouldn't accept, sir, that there is any group of paramilitaries or armed individuals that would escape these provisions, that are not intended to be covered by these provisions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: No, the provisions would cover everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we can turn the page over to page 6, I want to ask you about police -- or perhaps before we do that, sorry, we could just stay on page 5 for one last -- one last issue, because before the break you properly suggested that there had been a change as to whom the weapons could be given. And it says there in paragraph (c): "The weapons ... are to be placed in secure storage under a two-lock system, with one lock being controlled by UNPROFOR and the other by the president of the council of the opstina (district) concerned." Now, first of all, would you agree, just to be clear, that "opstina" is better translated as "municipality"?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I believe that's the translation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And do you have any understanding as to why it was decided that the key should be held by the president of the council of the opstina instead of, for example, anyone from the regional SBWS government?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: No. This is a military matter. I wouldn't have any intimate knowledge of why that was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let's look at a police matter if we turn the page. And again we see here the same provision. This actually, sir, is in all material elements identical to the provision from the Vance Plan which is paragraph 19 of the Vance Plan. But since we have this document in front of us and you prefer this one, let's use this one.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: No, it's not a question of whether I prefer it. It's a question of which instructions we were operating under. I had no choice in the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In the first full paragraph it says: "The local police forces are responsible to the existing opstina councils in the UNPAs. Any existing regional police structures can remain in place, provided they are consistent with the principle described above concerning the national composition of the local police forces." Do you have any understanding or knowledge as to why local police forces were to report to the opstina councils instead of, for example, to the regional structures?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: No, I don't have any idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can you recall the existence of any regional police structures?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: No, I cannot. Police matters were dealt with by civilian police. I had my hands full with civilian matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you need a JNA pass to move around Sector East?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: No. I was promised freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were other UN officials required to have a JNA pass --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- to move around?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have Prosecution tab 21 which is 05163, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Just to follow-up on my last question: Did you pass through JNA check-points when you travelled around Sector East?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And can you describe how frequently you came across JNA check-points? At what intervals were they placed along the roads if they were on the roads?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: That's truly very difficult to remember, Mr. Gosnell. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let's put it this way. At the outskirts, for example, of Erdut where you were residing at the time, did you pass through JNA check-points in all directions or only one direction or can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: There again I can't be sure because since we were never stopped, since we were assured freedom of movement, it was something that I wouldn't observe. It's a general principle in all UN peacekeeping operations that an essential part of our job is to have complete freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we can go to page 3 of this document down at the bottom and this is your -- this particular part of the document is your report -- at least you're the drafter of this report. It appears to be the 22nd of May, 1992. Down at the bottom of point 4 there it says -- and it's in reference to the Miklusevci expulsions that were carried out on the 18th of May, and just to situate us you say this was committed by persons from the Territorial Defence, local police in civilian clothes, and other armed persons after a night of terrorising the houses by gun-fire and grenades. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I don't -- as I've told you before, there was so many expulsions, I can't recall this particular event. But I may be able to cast some light on this to help you. I indeed was the drafter, but the releasing officer was the commanding officer of the sector, Colonel Khromchenkov, the Russian. These were probably his feelings or his information put in my words because his English was not very good. So I don't recall this particularly. If you give me a second, I'll try and help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not so much interested in attempting to parse out the distinction between these armed groups, but what I am interested in is down there at point 4 --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- and what you say there or perhaps on the instructions of Khromchenkov, you say: "Until total disarmament of Territorial Defence and all - repeat all - other armed persons takes place, it would be impossible to protect individual returnees without a massive UN presence." So can I take it from this that at this time, certainly, there has not been disarmament as foreseen in the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Can you give me the date of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The 22nd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: There was not complete disarmament. That didn't take place fully until my tenure ended on June 1st.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if, indeed, what we're dealing with is terrorisation by armed persons, it's not very likely, is it, that the local police carrying side-arms are going to be able to suppress that violence, is it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I suppose I could agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have Prosecution tab 23 which is 05172.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I make a further comment there, a further thought?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: The massive problem we had was that the police were playing a Jekyll and Hyde role. At one time they would be so-called local police and then the next minute they would be paramilitaries or at least people in different uniforms or in different clothes carrying weapons, but they were identified many, many times as policemen who were supposed to be protecting the very people they were expelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And since the opstina authorities are accorded authority over local police, it might be difficult to prevent, for example, local TOs from becoming suddenly local police?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have Prosecution tab 23 which is 05172, please. Page 3. And this is an outgoing code cable from Nambiar to Goulding. The date is the 25th of May, roughly the same time-period. And in the middle of the page it says: "Demobilisation of the territorials and irregulars is the next urgent task ..." Again, fairly clear indication, is it not, that there had not been demobilisation of forces as foreseen in the Vance Plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: There's a comment over on page 4 -- or, excuse me, on page 2, paragraph 4, which you refer to in your statement. And in your statement it's paragraph 89. "Our own reports show a basic climate of hostility and intimidation by the wilder Serbian elements towards the various national minorities in, now, especially Sector East ... we have the clear impression that actions in Sector East are not entirely home-grown ..." Do you have any understanding of what Nambiar meant when he says that the actions in Sector East are not entirely home grown?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: No, I don't know what he's trying to say there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You've told us a little bit about your contacts with the JNA. Can you tell us how frequent were your contacts with opstina authorities?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: The opstina authorities were sometimes very, very difficult to pin down. We had no regular meetings. I could set up group meetings from time to time. How often do I have meet with them? Once every two weeks, ten days, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, you describe a lot of -- in many of your reports, for example, going to Beli Manastir or travelling to other locations, and those frequent -- those reports are frequent. Would it be correct to say that the first person you would seek out when you go to one of these locations would, indeed, be the local opstina authorities?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And who would that be typically? Would it be a mayor? Would it be a chief of police?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Both. Sometimes -- generally speaking, it would be the mayor, but sometimes the chief of police would be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that whenever you moved around or -- well, let's not say always, but if you went into an area your purpose was, in fact, to meet with those local authorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: That would be -- my purpose would be to meet with someone, yes, or to witness an expulsion or the results of an expulsion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you see evidence that these opstinas were under strong central control or would you say that they were often acting as authorities unto themselves?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, could we break that down into two separate questions. I think the compound nature of it may be a bit confusing. It is to me at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I think it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, to me too. Could you answer the question, Mr. Lubin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I did see evidence that these opstinas were under strong central control because time and again when I made a suggestion to a local mayor or other local official, they said we would have to talk to Knin before we can give you an answer on that. And I think that's documented in either one of the documents attached to my report or in my statement itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, sir, that's an extremely surprising answer because I've looked at many of your reports, I've looked at your statement, and I've looked at many documents that are not in your report.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: What's surprising?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can you pin-point? Can you recall any circumstance in which someone said: I'll get in touch with Knin and then I'll decide what to do?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes. I can remember almost those exact words, they were used several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if that was the case then why not just ask Knin to issue or put pressure on Knin to issue blanket instructions to these various opstina that you were visiting in order to --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: That would be the task of my supervisor. I had no control over the other sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what was your purpose in meeting - again, if that's the case, that individuals were saying, We'll get in touch with Knin - why did you meet with Mr. Hadzic, Mr. Mladen Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Well, my job was civilian co-ordinator. I had to co-ordinate with local authorities. Whether they listened to me was up to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, do you consider Mr. -- Dr. Mladen Hadzic to be a local authority or do you consider him to be a regional authority?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I considered him to be a local authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what was his position?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I'm not sure of his title. I believe -- he wasn't the mayor, it was position above that, president of whatever the opstina was. I think we have his title here in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you have any notion of the geographical limits of the opstina that you say he was the head of?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes, I mean I can't point it out to you, but I think it's delineated on one of the maps we have, the opstinas. He would have been in the Erdut-Dalj region, that would be his opstina, excuse my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to take you now to some of these individual incidents of expulsion that you describe in your statement. The first one - and we can now remove the document from the screen - the first one is described -- well, not necessarily the first one, but let's say one is described at paragraph 47 of your statement. You describe buses arriving. They were painted blue-grey. Armed men dressed in some kind of camouflage uniform but lacking any distinctive identifying features moved people on board." Now, how would you characterise the identity of those individuals or can you in any way characterise their affiliation beyond what you've said in the statement?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: This was the first expulsion I witnessed in person. If you go back to the previous couple of paragraphs, you will see that I just arrived in the sector. I think it was late in the day and I received a message from UN -- ICRC, yes, I remember. And they called me and asked me to go immediately to the scene. The scene was as I described. What was your question again, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let me put this specific question to you --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- did you see that the men with guns were using those guns to threaten people to get on the buses --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- or were they not doing that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: The people were already on the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you didn't?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I didn't see the beginning of the expulsion. I saw the buses as they were about to leave, and I got on board and I talked to people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you can't say whether the armed men were at that location at that time forcing people to get on the buses rather than that individuals may have been intimidated, coerced, threatened at some earlier time which then induced them to get on the bus?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: At that particular occasion I didn't see who was forcing them to get on the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But you see, sir, the distinction I'm trying to get at and it goes back --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- it goes back to the dilemma that we were discussing earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the speakers not to overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand whether they were physically forced, induced onto the bus, or whether they went there because of some prior acts of threats or coercion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell and Mr. Lubin, did you hear the intervention of the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did but I didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The interpreters asked not to overlap, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So the question is whether on this occasion, we're speaking of this occasion, it was the case that they had been threatened at some earlier time which induced them to get on the buses, in a sense, voluntarily; or whether they had been forced on to those buses by the individuals with guns who were there?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Well, I can categorically state that they were never in any sense put on the buses in a voluntary matter. The second part of that question is whether they had been forced on those buses by those individuals I don't know because I arrived later on the scene. This was the first population movement that I witnessed personally. After this, I immediately contacted Hadzic's office, this is the local Hadzic, to set up a procedure where this kind of thing would never happen again. If there was a so-called voluntary movement of population, his office was to give us at least 24 hours' notice, allow us freely to speak to the expellees, to see if their movement was voluntary, and to perhaps understand why they were signing over every possession they owned to the local government, including expensive farm equipment and all their personal belongings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I'm required under the Rules to tell you that of course we contest that claim, but I'm not going to do it chapter and verse with you here. But what I do want to go through with you is the content of your statement in order to try and understand it. And you say here that: "The expellees were terrified, they were mostly old people, women, and children. The children were crying. I asked if they were going willingly, but all were too afraid to answer. It was clear to all present that they were not going willingly. They had only small bundles or clothes or hand baggage and were leaving behind everything that they possessed, homes, furniture, livestock, and farm equipment, in summary, their every possession." Now, does that description correspond to what you observed in respect of the Hungarian refugees from Baranja as well?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: No, as I mentioned before, the Hungarian refugees was an exception to the rule. They had been informed a couple of days beforehand and were prepared to leave, they wished to leave because they were being threatened. You know, their -- I must interject something here, Mr. Gosnell. There are so many forms of violence. There's mental torture, there are subliminal threats, there is sleep deprivation because of these threats, the whole atmosphere in the region I can only describe as toxic. You could feel the hatred in the air. It was an awful time to be present there, and referring back to this particular expulsion which you have asked me about, that was my first encounter with such savagery. And, quite frankly, I was in shock. I didn't think civilised people behaved in that way anymore. I thought we were rid of that when we got rid of the Nazi regime in the Second World War, but apparently we didn't. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, sir, I don't want to argue with you, but we're here talking about individual responsibility. That's what this case and this trial is about. And what I'm trying to pin-point here, it's a fairly small point but it's important in this context -- and I take on board entirely what you've said. But in this context what I want to ask you is whether you view the characteristics surrounding these individuals to be different from the characteristics that you saw in respect of the individuals whom you assisted to leave Baranja?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Explain the word "characteristics."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The notion that the expellees were terrified, that they were crying, that they were -- that they were afraid, that they were not going willingly in some general sense even if at that moment in time they wished to depart for security reasons, and that they had only small bundles or clothes or hand baggage, and that they were leaving behind everything they possessed. Just those are the attributes that I'm asking you about, whether those attributes were shared in respect of the individuals in Baranja.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: In general terms, yes, except for the bundles of clothes. The Hungarian refugees had a few more belongings, suitcases, et cetera, they had more time to pack. But the atmosphere surrounding both expulsions, their feelings were the same. They were in distress. You have to understand that these people'd lived there all their lives, this is where they're home. They were so-called Hungarians, but they were being banished to Hungary, a country they didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can we have 1D230, which is Defence tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, this is a statement from an individual who left Dalj at around this time. And if we can go to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what is the date of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It's a statement that was given several -- many years after the events --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- several years after the events --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Which event are we talking -- excuse me, sir --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I -- could I just get some guidance from Mr. Gosnell regarding this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It's from Prosecution disclosure as I -- well, apparently it's -- I can't say for sure whether it's from Prosecution disclosure, but I can say that it was obtained from either the Prosecution or the Croatian authorities directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Well, to the extent this is a witness statement gathered for the purposes of prosecution -- local prosecution or prosecution by this institution, we object to the showing of it to the witness. I believe that we've had a standing protocol where we're quoting from the document and not showing it to the witness. I'm happy to be corrected on that score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is it a witness statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- for this jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, are we right when we think that you are going to show a particular passage from this document to the witness and then ask a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This person says: "I was still in Dalj a year" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, that is exactly -- you show it to the witness, the passage, you don't read it into the record, and you ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's fair enough, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, you've heard the instruction from the President. I'm interested in that first paragraph, and this person seems to be indicating that he had been previously prohibited from leaving by someone on the Serb side and he was waiting for UNPROFOR to arrive precisely so he could leave. Now, would you agree that -- and I'm not sure that we disagree at all, Mr. Lubin. But would you agree that there would be circumstances in which a climate could arise that individuals from Dalj, Erdut, Aljmas, would genuinely wish to get out of there?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Let me go back to your first point, Mr. Gosnell. You say that the person was waiting for us before they left. That's -- it doesn't say that -- your interpretation's wrong I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's a fair point to make. I can't say that he says that they were waiting --

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: For someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It says that they coincided, does it not?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: No, it's just giving a date in time in my opinion, "I only left when UNPROFOR arrived," they're giving you a specific time-frame. That's the only reading I can make of that. Maybe you have a different interpretation, but I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Forgive me, perhaps I am being too impatient, but did Defence counsel plan on reading the or directing the witness to the third sentence as well? Because I think without that there is a misperception on the record about what information is contained in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I suppose the witness reads or should read the entire paragraph, not only the first or the second or the third sentence, but the entire paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I would be very content with that, Mr. President, and then I would propose to ask a question, but my question is based on the content of what's in that paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No problem with that, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And I do believe I'm allowed to characterise to some degree without misstating it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the question, sir, is whether you see here that this individual appears to be saying - without getting into too much of a discussion of rhetoric or language - he appears to be saying that he wasn't able to leave before the arrival of UNPROFOR, that he wished to, but that then when UNPROFOR arrived he was able to. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: There again, Mr. Gosnell, with the greatest respect, it was a woman who is saying this. She's talking about "my husband." But you've probably said the words correctly, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in respect of a person like this, there would be no question of needing to force them on to a bus at gunpoint to leave; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Judging by what's happened before, and particularly to her husband, I can well understand why she volunteered to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the Prosecution would oppose the admission of this document. It is a statement. We have certain procedures that we follow in order to admit statements, and I don't believe any of them have been satisfied. The Defence has shown the witness one paragraph, asked the witness to comment on counsel's interpretation of essentially the first sentence, and we think it would be inappropriate to admit this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If I may just briefly, Mr. President. Given the nature of the exhibits that have been tendered with this witness, including a large quantity of statements that were not only not given to a judicial authority but to goodness knows whom -- that's going too far, they do indicate who it was given to. The point being that there are innumerable statements attached to this witness's testimony. I think it's not inappropriate for the purposes of impeachment do the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think that in order to avoid painting ourselves into a corner we will come back to that tomorrow or eventually even in a written decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So the document is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit D33, marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 05928, please, which is Prosecution tab 28.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I make a comment on Mr. Gosnell's last statement, please? A point of clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, you just said given the nature of the exhibits that have been tendered with this witness, including a large majority of the statements that were not only given to -- that were not only not given to a judicial authority. Let me point out that all those statements, police statements which are attached to my testimony, would have been given to local police authorities for their action. And in that regard, at one point in June 1992 I received a personal letter from the chief of police in UNPROFOR that some 650 cases had been forward to local police authorities and at that time not one was being investigated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, unless that's in the statement I suggest we strike the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Fair enough. Then let's move on to the document before us, and this is dated the 19th of April, 1992. And it concerns an alleged expulsion through Nemetin -- to Nemetin via Sarvas. And it appears that this expulsion occurred during the night I believe of the previous night. And here you say: "Under existing circumstances situation cannot be controlled by UNPROFOR as expulsions are during darkness ..." Can you enlighten us as to what the security situation was at night relative to during the day in this area?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: No, I can't because the JNA imposed a curfew and we were not allowed to patrol after nightfall. May I just ask you one other question on your statement there, Mr. Gosnell? Can I ask you why you say "alleged expulsion"? Because these expulsions absolutely took place. They're not a figment of our imaginations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When did the JNA curfew come into effect, as best you can recall?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: The JNA curfew was in effect all -- most of the time I was there. I believe it was removed later on in the mission and I think that's also noted in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And was it your observation that they were controlling movement during the curfew?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: I can't make an observation on that because I was not allowed out at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It says here: "JNA is not controlling situation and local police do not make night patrols." Did you ever inquire as to whether or not the police were permitted to make night patrols in accordance with the JNA curfew?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you ever hear?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Where -- when you say "police," which police are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Whichever police you're referring to down at the bottom of the page in your report.

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: Could you direct me to that, Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's the very last line here if we can scroll -- well, it's there. "JNA is not controlling situation and local police do not make night patrols."

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: If I said that, then it must be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I understand that it's correct or I accept that it's correct, I don't disagree. What I'm asking you is whether you ever heard that the police were not permitted to make patrols in accordance with this curfew?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that. It wouldn't make any sense, they were one and the same body. They were both Yugoslav authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you don't see that there might be any distinction between the JNA and local police in terms of control, in terms of capacity, in terms of decision-making, in terms of ability to suppress violence?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that, did I?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, do you -- the question was - and let's just go back to the question and maybe you can just answer the question and then we'll move on to the next question - did you ever hear whether the police were permitted, according to the terms of the curfew, to conduct patrols at night?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And I would submit that the question has been asked and answered in line 16 on page 93: "No, I didn't hear that."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The -- could we have 05929, Prosecution tab 29, please. Now, this -- we've looked at this document before and now we're looking at it again. This again is in respect of the Dalj expulsion or alleged expulsion on the 18th and 19th of April. Now, here it seems from your report that your first -- the first person on the Serb side who you seek out in order to address the situation is the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES LUBIN
utterances.text: The JNA were ever present in our camp. There was always an officer, a liaison officer, in an office nearby. So that would be the person I would contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we go to P191, please, Prosecution tab 78. This should not be broadcast and I believe we need to move into closed session -- private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So, Mr. Lubin, we finish for the day. We will be back in court with you tomorrow at 9.00, same courtroom. I remind you that you are still under oath, which means that you cannot discuss your testimony with anybody and that you cannot talk to any of the parties. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If there's nothing else we can deal with in the next two minutes, court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
